subtype: Witnessing an event and then reading reports [Actor]
passage: Jomon here, Seema's classmate. We were both at the college junction on Tuesday when an auto nudged a scooter. Nobody was hurt; the scooter rider just picked up a broken mirror. That night our class group chat was full of it. A forwarded post said the auto driver was on his phone and jumped the red. By Thursday, Seema was telling our lab partners the whole thing: "I saw him on the phone, he didn't even look." She said it with total certainty, tapping the table. I didn't see a phone. I remember both hands on the handlebar and the light turning amber. When I said so, she laughed. "You were looking at your chai." Maybe I was. But she was looking at the scooter first; I saw her turn. I don't know what she saw. I only know her version grew after the chat.

qa.q: What did the forwarded post in the class group chat say?
qa.a: That the auto driver was on his phone and jumped the red.

qa.q: What does Seema tapping the table and laughing off Jomon suggest about her state of mind?
qa.a: Seema felt completely certain of her version, so Jomon's doubt seemed silly to her rather than something worth checking.

qa.q: What could Seema have done when Jomon remembered the light and the hands differently?
qa.a: Pause and sort out which parts she saw at the junction and which she first read in the chat, before retelling it as fact.

qa.q: How is the auto driver affected if Seema's version spreads?
qa.a: The driver could be blamed for using a phone and jumping the red even if that never happened, just because a confident witness repeated a forwarded claim.

grounding: A young woman who saw a small accident absorbs details from a forwarded post and retells them with full certainty.

subtype: Witnessing an event and then reading reports [Actor]
passage: Monday. Ira is waiting for the tram outside the library when a cyclist wobbles and falls beside a parked car. It happens in two seconds. She notices a scraped elbow, a spilled bag of apples, a door swinging. She is not sure what hit what. Wednesday. A neighbourhood news page posts: "Cyclist hurt by speeding white van near library." The comments add a honking horn and a driver who sped off. Ira reads it twice on the tram and nods along. The next Monday, her friend Pema asks what happened. Ira answers without a pause: the white van, the horn, the driver racing away. "I saw it myself." Pema scrolls to a photo she took that day: a blue parked car, its door wide open, no van anywhere. Ira stares. "But I remember the horn," she says, quieter.

qa.q: What was in the photo Pema took that day?
qa.a: A blue parked car, its door wide open, and no van anywhere.

qa.q: How did Ira feel when she said "But I remember the horn" more quietly?
qa.a: Shaken and unsure 😰 The horn felt like a real memory, yet the photo showed that her certainty had been built partly from the news post and comments.

qa.q: At which point could Ira have protected her own memory, and how?
qa.a: On that first Monday, by noting what she actually saw (a scraped elbow, apples, a swinging door, not sure what hit what) before reading Wednesday's post.

qa.q: How might the cyclist be affected if people trust Ira's confident version?
qa.a: The cyclist's account of the opened car door might be doubted, and blame could fall on a van that was never there.

grounding: A young adult witness blends a news post and comments into her memory of a fall until she is certain of details she never saw.

subtype: Witnessing an event and then reading reports [Actor]
passage: Mehak, you asked why I say "I think" so often. When I was nineteen, my friend Usha and I saw a bus scrape a cycle-rickshaw outside our college gate. The rickshaw lost a wheel, the rickshaw-wala shouted, and that was all. Next morning the newspaper said the rickshaw had overturned and a schoolboy was hurt. Our hostel buzzed with it, everyone adding a crying boy, a bleeding knee. For thirty years I told that story, and I could see the boy: his blue shorts, his lost tiffin box. Then at a reunion Usha laughed. "Sonali, there was no boy. I was holding your arm. We watched a wheel roll into the drain." I went home that night and could still see those blue shorts. So now, beta, I say "I think."

qa.q: What did Usha say at the reunion?
qa.a: "Sonali, there was no boy."

qa.q: Why might Sonali still see the blue shorts even after the reunion?
qa.a: Sonali probably felt shaken, because the detail had been told and pictured so often over thirty years that it felt like a true memory, even after Usha said it never happened.

qa.q: What choice did Sonali make after learning the truth, and why does it help?
qa.a: To say "I think" more often, which leaves room for the chance that even a vivid memory is wrong.

qa.q: How might Mehak react the next time an accident story spreads in a group chat?
qa.a: Mehak may be slower to trust vivid details that arrive later through chats and news, remembering how Sonali's clear picture of the boy turned out to be false.

grounding: An elder recalls how, at nineteen, a newspaper report and hostel talk added a hurt boy to a minor accident the elder had witnessed.

subtype: Witnessing an event and then reading reports [Actor]
passage: Dechen was already late for her exam, running down the hairpin road in Gangtok with rain dripping off her hood, when a jeep slid on the wet bend and tapped a parked scooter. A crunch, a shout, and she was past, umbrella low. By evening, the town's news group said the jeep had been speeding and the driver "smelled of drink." Someone posted a photo of a dented scooter from a different angle. By Thursday Dechen was telling her cousin Pema, "I saw it. He was flying round the bend." Pema raised an eyebrow. "You told me you had your head down and were running." Dechen opened her mouth. She could see the speed clearly. She was sure. Wasn't she?

qa.q: Where was Dechen running when she saw the jeep?
qa.a: Down the hairpin road in Gangtok, late for her exam.

qa.q: How does Dechen feel when Pema reminds her she was running with her head down?
qa.a: She is suddenly unsure; the speed felt perfectly clear, yet she realises her certainty may come from the news group, not her eyes.

qa.q: What could Dechen do before telling the story again?
qa.a: She could separate what she actually saw in those two seconds from what the group posts added, and say "I only glimpsed it."

qa.q: How might the jeep driver be affected if Dechen's version spreads?
qa.a: The driver could be blamed for speeding and drinking on the strength of a confident story from someone who only glimpsed the bend.

grounding: A young adult who glimpsed a minor accident absorbs later posts into her memory and feels certain.

subtype: Witnessing an event and then reading reports [Actor]
passage: Deepak was coming out of the metro station in Hyderabad when a delivery rider's scooter clipped the bumper of a car at the signal. Nobody fell. Words, a honk, done. That night the colony group lit up: a black SUV, an abusive driver, the rider knocked down. Deepak read every message. At breakfast he told his sister Mahima, "I was right there. Big black SUV. The man got out and shouted at the boy." Mahima scrolled on her phone. "The traffic police posted the clip." It showed a small silver hatchback. The driver got out, raised both hands and apologised. Deepak watched it twice. "But I saw…" he began, and stopped. He had been so sure.

qa.q: What did the traffic police clip actually show?
qa.a: It showed a small silver hatchback, and the driver raised both hands and apologised.

qa.q: What does Deepak's stopping mid-sentence suggest he is realising?
qa.a: He feels shaken and confused as he realises details from the colony group had slipped into his memory, and that feeling sure didn't make it accurate.

qa.q: What would you advise Deepak before he shares what he saw next time?
qa.a: Note down what he saw right away, before reading group messages, and say "this is what I noticed" rather than stating it as fact.

qa.q: How does Mahima's approach shape the moment for Deepak?
qa.a: By showing the clip calmly instead of arguing, she lets him see the gap himself, without feeling mocked.

grounding: A young adult who saw a minor accident adopts details from chat messages and feels wrongly certain.
